How it works

Every source is free and public, and nothing is filled in between reports.

  1. Collect

    A collector reads AISStream receivers, IMF PortWatch, the EIA, Polymarket, the IMO register and six named publishers, each on its own schedule.

  2. Check

    Every six hours a review adds new war events, and only those with a linked report. Claims made by one side stay marked as claims.

  3. Show

    Each panel shows its own date. A missing price, position or count stays missing, and nothing is estimated in between.

Read the method

Every ship, strike and price on one map. Dated, sourced and never guessed.

Questions

Is Passage free to use?

Yes. There is no sign in, no cookie and no analytics, and every source Passage reads is free and public.

Where do the ship positions come from?

From two free feeds of coastal receivers: AISStream, and AISHub contributors relayed by Open Waters AIS about a minute behind. Each ship's card names the feed its position came from. Together they cover part of the Strait of Hormuz and almost none of Bab el-Mandeb, so the map shows what those receivers hear, not every ship at sea.

Why does the strait sometimes look empty?

Tankers often switch AIS off near attacks, and the free receivers sit on the coast, far from parts of the shipping lanes. A feed can also stop sending for a whole region, as AISStream did in October 2026. An empty map does not mean an empty strait.

How current is each figure?

Ship positions refresh every 10 seconds and fade after 10 minutes; those relayed by Open Waters arrive about a minute after they were sent. War events are reviewed every six hours. Oil closes arrive a day later from the EIA, and PortWatch releases transit counts weekly, so the latest day is often several days old.

What counts as a war event?

A dated attack or strike in the region with at least one linked report. Events reported by only one side are marked as claimed, and incidents from the IMO register are placed from their own text.

Does Passage say an event moved the oil price?

No. Each event shows Brent and the related odds on the day and a few days later. Prices move for many reasons, so this is what happened next, not what caused it.

What is an AIS gap?

A ship that stops reporting for three hours or more while moving deep inside reliable reception. It is evidence that AIS was switched off, not proof.

Can I use the data?

Each source keeps its own terms, listed on the method page. Passage links every event to its original report and does not republish full articles.
